source_read: NCBI Bookshelf HTML full text, NBK621252 (National Vital Statistics Reports 75(1), all sections) and its Table A page (all years 2017-2023), read in my own browser tab; Tables B, C and the rate table not needed for any claim number; all editors' arithmetic recomputed

claims.overstatement: Minor: 'wrote it anywhere on the certificate' is broader than the method, which searches three literal-text fields (Part I causes, Part II contributing conditions, and how the injury occurred); the magnitude states this exactly. The report names X85 'homicide' (the claim's 'assault' is the ICD-10 category title). The definition is stated for decedents who resided and died in the US.
claims.note: Editors' arithmetic recomputed from Table A: 2023 top-15 counts sum to 179,965 against n = 106,352 (1.692); 2017 top-15 counts sum to 103,675 against n = 70,715 (1.466, so 1.47). Both correct. The two sets of 15 drugs differ (2017 includes diazepam and tramadol; 2023 xylazine and bromazolam), and drugs outside the top 15 are not in the sums, so the ratio understates total multiple counting; deaths with no specific drug are in the denominator. ICD-10 grouping examples (fentanyl with tramadol in T40.4; oxycodone with codeine and morphine in T40.2) are in the Introduction. 'Minimum' and 'cannot be determined which drug caused' both confirmed.

anchors.locator: Data and Methods > Data source and study population, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Population: decedents who resided and died in the US with underlying cause X40-X44 (unintentional), X60-X64 (suicide), X85 (homicide) or Y10-Y14 (undetermined intent), reflecting acute intoxication; deaths from chronic exposure (such as liver toxicity) and adverse effects at therapeutic or prophylactic dosages excluded. Manner: unintentional 87%-93%, suicide 4%-7%, undetermined 3%-5%, homicide 0.2%.

ICD-10 codes may reflect broad drug categories: fentanyl, Demerol, tramadol, nitazenes and Suboxone all fall in T40.4 'other synthetic narcotics'; oxycodone is generally coded T40.2 'other opioids', which also holds codeine and morphine. NCHS therefore searches the literal text written by the certifier, usually a medical examiner or coroner in overdose deaths, in three fields: Part I causes, Part II contributing conditions, and how the injury occurred.

anchors.locator: Data and Methods > Identifying drug mentions and involvement of the drug in the death, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
anchors.extracted: A drug mentioned in the literal text is assumed to be involved in the death unless context says otherwise (examples: an MRSA infection phrase, or 'not drug related').

Counts per referent drug are not mutually exclusive; a death with several drugs is counted in every relevant category (example: cocaine and heroin). Drug-specific counts and rates may be undercounts and should be taken as the minimum, because the drug may not have been written in the literal text.

2023 (n = 106,352): fentanyl 73,297; methamphetamine 34,167; cocaine 31,700; xylazine 6,096; alprazolam 4,642; oxycodone 4,142; heroin 4,071; gabapentin 4,027; amphetamine 3,658; methadone 3,451; diphenhydramine 2,616; morphine 2,345; hydrocodone 2,043; clonazepam 1,976; bromazolam 1,734; sum 179,965 (editors' arithmetic, 1.69 per death). 2017 (n = 70,715): top-15 sum 103,675 (1.47). Notes: a death with more than one drug is counted in each total.

anchors.locator: Discussion > Data considerations and study limitations, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Overdose deaths often involve several drugs; for such deaths the literal-text analysis cannot determine whether one drug or a combination caused the death.

claims.note: 12.3% (2017) and 4.0% (2023) recomputed as 100 - 87.7 and 100 - 96.0: correct. The measure is deaths with no multiple-cause code in T36.0-T50.8 (a drug or a drug class), as the claim says; the Discussion words the same figures more loosely as 'at least one specific drug', and Table A's note rounds them to 88% and 96%. A class code (for example T40.2) is not a specific drug, so the share naming no specific drug is higher than 4.0% and is not reported. 'Should not be carried to later years' is the claim's inference; the report itself warns that improved reporting may influence trends. The Discussion also states that certifiers differ in listing one drug or several, and that testing varies, which bears on the claim's first sentence and on 'do not show which deaths had toxicology'.

anchors.locator: Data and Methods > Measuring the percentage of specific drugs on death certificates, 1st paragraph; Results, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Specificity measure: share of overdose deaths with one or more multiple-cause codes T36.0-T50.8. It rose every year: 87.7% (2017), 92.0%, 93.8%, 94.4%, 95.2%, 95.8%, 96.0% (2023); so 12.3% and 4.0% without such a code (editors' arithmetic). Improved reporting could influence trends for specific drugs.

anchors.locator: Discussion > Data considerations and study limitations, 2nd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Reporting of at least one specific drug improved from 87.7% (2017) to 96.0% (2023); some increases may be partly due to better reporting, and better reporting could obscure true decreases.

anchors.locator: Discussion > Data considerations and study limitations, 3rd paragraph and bullets 'Variation in death investigations and reporting' and 'Determination of which drugs to report'; 4th and 5th paragraphs
anchors.extracted: Literal-text quality varies with investigation systems: whether toxicology is done and what is tested vary by jurisdiction, decedent and time; some certifiers write a single lethal drug, others several, and software space limits can stop all contributing drugs being written. Results are minimums because drugs not written are not counted; rare drugs missing from the search list are a further source of undercount.
Literal-text search was built to get past the broad ICD-10 drug codes; counts are minimums because a drug involved but not written in the literal text cannot be found.

anchors.locator: Discussion > Data considerations and study limitations, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: For deaths involving several drugs, the analysis cannot determine whether one drug or a combination caused the death.

anchors.locator: Data and Methods > Data source and study population, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Deaths from chronic drug exposure (such as liver toxicity) and from adverse effects at therapeutic or prophylactic dosages are not included.

claims.note: The report states this as a possibility ('could'), not a measured bias; the claim keeps it conditional ('may reflect'). Context not used by the claim: national heroin-involved deaths fell from 16,085 (2017) to 4,071 (2023) and morphine from 6.9% to 2.2% of overdose deaths (Table A; Results bullets), and the report judges falls in specific drugs likely to be true decreases.

anchors.locator: Discussion > Data considerations and study limitations, bullet 'Attribution to a specific drug' (after the 3rd paragraph)
anchors.extracted: Drugs that share metabolites, or are metabolites of others, can be misattributed: a morphine mention could refer to heroin, since morphine is a heroin metabolite, which could understate heroin-involved deaths and overstate morphine-involved deaths.

anchors.locator: Discussion > Data considerations and study limitations, bullet 'Interpretation of toxicology results'
anchors.extracted: Interpretation depends on which tests were ordered, the characteristics of the causative agents and their metabolites, and other investigation evidence.
